title: Most Servers on the Planet Are Vulnerable to This Firmware Code-Execution Flaw
gist: CVE-2026-97631, a 9.5-severity 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE boot ICMP handler of TianoCore EDK II, lets attackers with local network access run ring-0 code before Secure Boot and TPM defenses load, affecting firmware used by most server vendors. Discovered by Anthropic and Google researchers, its embargo was broken months early by an AMI pull request, leaving defenders with a public patch, unclear vendor exposure and a likely 'forever' bug.

insights.claim: CVE-2026-97631, rated 9.5 out of 10, sits in TianoCore EDK II, the open-source reference code that virtually all UEFI suppliers including AMI, Insyde and Phoenix use, and in Microsoft's hardened Project Mu fork.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Monoculture in firmware reference code means one bug spans most of the global server fleet.
insights.quote: Virtually all UEFI suppliers (sometimes still called IBVs or independent BIOS vendors), including AMI, Insyde, and Phoenix, use the reference code extensively.
insights.locator: The vulnerability, with a severity rating

insights.claim: The flaw is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE Base Code driver: it fails to enforce a 504-byte copy limit for ICMP error messages and advances the destination pointer by cumulative rather than per-fragment length, letting attacker bytes overwrite adjacent memory.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Long-lived legacy code paths in boot stacks remain under-audited despite prior fuzzing campaigns.
insights.quote: CVE-2026-97631 is a 16-year-old buffer overflow in the PXE-Base Code driver

insights.claim: Exploit code runs in ring 0 before the OS and Secure Boot load and bypasses attestation, enabling attackers to install further payloads that run early in every boot despite the initial payload lacking persistence.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Pre-boot compromise undermines hardware attestation, a cornerstone of confidential computing and cloud trust.

insights.claim: An attacker with short-term network access could use the bug to hijack boot flow while the TPM is still accessible, potentially breaking disk encryption, and theft scenarios would make it even easier.
insights.speaker: HD Moore
insights.so_what: Disk-encryption guarantees tied to TPM measured boot are weaker than assumed on PXE-enabled fleets.
insights.quote: This could be used to break disk encryption for cases where an attacker has short-term network access
insights.locator: This vulnerability in the ICMP parser

insights.claim: The malicious ICMP error can be delivered by simple unicast from any network distance to the target IP during PXE boot, causing denial of service by hanging boot or code execution if the firmware build is known.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Network-boot windows in data centers are an exploitable attack surface that should be segmented.
insights.locator: The malicious error can be delivered

insights.claim: Researchers Alex Matrosov of Anthropic and Dan Holmes of Google discovered the flaw and planned coordinated disclosure in January, but AMI published a pull request with the fix last month, forcing TianoCore to issue a public advisory early.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: AI-lab security researchers are now finding critical infrastructure bugs; embargo discipline across vendors is fragile.

insights.claim: With patch code public, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the bug is triggered and build exploits, while patching UEFI across millions of devices from thousands of vendors is slow.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Expect a prolonged exposure window and elevated nation-state and ransomware exploitation risk.
insights.quote: With publicly available patch code, it will be trivial for advanced hackers to learn how the vulnerability is triggered and to build working exploits.

insights.claim: This disclosure came six days after another botched disclosure of a critical code-execution flaw in PHP, suggesting a pattern of embargo failures.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Coordinated vulnerability disclosure processes are under strain, raising defenders' costs.

insights.claim: Given its ubiquity, CVE-2026-97631 is likely a forever bug that will live on in end-of-support systems.
insights.speaker: HD Moore
insights.so_what: Legacy server fleets carry permanent latent firmware risk; supports demand for firmware security and hardware refresh.

insights.claim: Unlike BootHole, BlackLotus and Baton Drop, this flaw needs only a basic code fix via a BIOS/UEFI update, without key revocations, dbx updates or OS media changes.
insights.speaker: Jesse Michael
insights.so_what: Remediation is operationally simpler than past Secure Boot bypasses, though still bottlenecked by firmware rollout.
insights.quote: this vulnerability can be fixed with a basic code fix, which will require deploying a BIOS/UEFI update

insights.claim: Exploitation requires guessing target-specific memory addresses, so exploits must be tuned per model, version and configuration rather than working universally.
insights.speaker: Jesse Michael
insights.so_what: Mass exploitation is less likely; targeted attacks by sophisticated actors are the main risk.
insights.quote: it needs to be tuned for each target model/version/configuration since the addresses will change based on those

insights.claim: Despite PixieFail prompting multiple fuzzing projects on EDK2's PXE code, those efforts failed to find this similar flaw.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Fuzzing alone is insufficient for firmware assurance; AI-assisted code review may fill the gap.
insights.quote: It appears those efforts failed to find this latest flaw.

insights.claim: The bug requires local network control and PXE boot (on by default), so it does not affect home users or devices booting only from disk; it mainly threatens insiders, nation-states and ransomware operators seeking privilege escalation.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Risk concentrates in enterprise and cloud data centers using network boot.
insights.locator: There are important caveats and limitations

insights.claim: Intel and Arm said their products are not directly affected, yet both companies' publicly available firmware references or borrows heavily from EDK2, and AMD, Phoenix, AMI, Microsoft and Amazon did not respond.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Vendor denials should be treated skeptically; OEM-integrated code may still carry the flaw.
insights.quote: CVE-2026-97631 is not directly applicable to Arm’s product portfolio.

insights.claim: Recommended mitigation is to ask firmware makers for guidance, temporarily disable network boot where possible, and monitor logs, since TPM and Secure Boot do not protect against this threat.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Operators face near-term operational trade-offs in provisioning workflows.
insights.locator: Those affected should check with the maker
